869.title: Love has boundaries
869.hook: love doesn't require letting yourself be harmed
869.howItsDone: Christians often point to the Gospel scenes where Jesus withdraws to pray as a pattern for rest and retreat, and people on many paths keep a sabbath, a quiet hour or a retreat as a protected time apart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love unreturned, and Leah turning from hoping to praise. Your line was still love. Did you manage to call an old love by its real name? Today, love that knows where it ends. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

People were coming and going, more of them than anyone could greet. In the Gospel of Mark, the disciples have just come back and told Jesus all they had done and taught, and the place is so busy, the text says, that they had no leisure so much as to eat. Nobody would blame a teacher for saying keep going, there's more to do. Instead Jesus says something else, and it's worth hearing on a day when the phone keeps buzzing and someone always needs one more thing. Today: love has boundaries.
screen: `COMING AND GOING.` → `NO LEISURE SO MUCH AS TO EAT.` → `JESUS SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the King James text Jesus tells them: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." Apart. Rest. In the middle of real need, with real people waiting. The Gospel doesn't treat this as a failure of love. It treats it as part of the work. Second, his own habit. Luke's Gospel says, in a short line, "he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed." The same teacher who healed and fed and taught also walked away from the crowd, on purpose. Christians read this in more than one way, but the plain picture is a person whose love had a shape, with edges, with times of being unavailable. Third, the harder edge. When Jesus sends his followers out, Matthew's Gospel has him tell them that where a house or a city won't receive them, they should leave, and shake off the dust of their feet. Not fight. Not stay and be ground down. Leave, and keep the peace inside. Some readers find a principle in it: you can wish someone well and still walk out of their door. Fourth, what this means on an ordinary day. Love doesn't require letting yourself be harmed. A boundary isn't a wall to punish someone. It's a line that tells the truth about what you can carry. Saying no to one thing can be the way you keep saying yes to the people you love. And if anyone listening is in a situation where love is being used to hurt them, a boundary may mean getting help from someone you trust. That too can be love, including love for yourself.
screen: `COME APART, AND REST A WHILE.` · `HE WITHDREW HIMSELF, AND PRAYED.` · `SHAKE OFF THE DUST.` · `A LINE THAT TELLS THE TRUTH.` · then, large: `LOVE HAS BOUNDARIES.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop. Breathe in, and feel where your body ends: your skin, the chair under you, the floor under your feet. That edge isn't unkind. It's just where you are. Now bring to mind one place in your life where a healthy boundary is needed. A time of day, a kind of request, a conversation that keeps going wrong. Don't plan a speech. Just let one clear sentence form, something simple you could say. Hold it gently, without anger. If you pray, you can ask for courage in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Love has boundaries. Love that has a shape, with times apart and lines it won't cross, the way Jesus withdrew to rest and pray. Today's word.
Your line: love has edges. Today, keep one healthy boundary kindly: a no said warmly, a phone set face down, a rest you don't apologize for. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

shake off the dust of your feet

he tells them to come apart into a desert place and rest a while.
Luke describes Jesus withdrawing into the wilderness to pray
"he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed."
a boundary has to be a punishment
the lesson calls it a line that tells the truth about what you can carry.

fork.setup: you're with the disciples. the crowds won't stop, and nobody has had time to eat. what does Jesus say?
options: stay, there's more to do.
come apart and rest a while.
send everyone home angry.
fork.reveal: "come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while." in the middle of real need, he gives rest.

trapdoor: what you thought: real love never says no.
what it means: love has a shape, with rest, time apart and lines it won't cross, and it doesn't require being harmed.
what a scholar hears: Mark 6:31's rest a while, Luke 5:16's withdrawing to pray, and Matthew 10:14's shaking off the dust, read together as love with edges.

870.title: Loving yourself rightly
870.hook: as yourself assumes you care for yourself too
870.howItsDone: In Buddhaghosa's instructions, loving-kindness practice begins by wishing oneself well before widening to others, and Jews study Hillel's sayings in Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's collection of the sages' teachings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love has boundaries: come apart and rest a while. Your line was love has edges. Which edge did you manage to keep? Today, the person inside those edges. Day eight hundred seventy.

A king and a queen are talking privately, and the king asks her a question that sounds almost dangerous. Is there anyone, he says, dearer to you than yourself? A careful wife might be expected to say: you, my lord. She doesn't. She says no, there is no one dearer to her than herself, and then she asks him the same question. He gives the same answer. Then the king goes to the Buddha and tells him what they said. What the Buddha does with their honesty is the surprise. Today: loving yourself rightly.
screen: `ANYONE DEARER THAN YOURSELF?` → `NO, SAYS THE QUEEN.` → `THE KING ASKS THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: First, the story. It comes from the Pali scriptures, and the couple are King Pasenadi of Kosala and Queen Mallika. When the king brings their conversation to the Buddha, the Buddha doesn't scold either of them. In the text he answers with a short verse. In plain words: search in every direction with your mind, and you will find no one dearer to anyone than their own self. Second, the turn. The verse doesn't stop there. Because each person holds themselves dear in just this way, it says, one who loves oneself should not harm another. Self-love, in this teaching, isn't the opposite of kindness. It's the doorway. Each person knows from the inside how much they want to be safe and well. That knowledge is the teacher. Third, a line from the Torah that makes a similar move. Leviticus says, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." As thyself. The command assumes there's a self being loved, a measure already in place. If the measure is broken, the neighbor gets a broken measure too. Fourth, a teacher from the Jewish tradition who held both sides at once. The sage Hillel is remembered in the Mishnah for three questions. In plain words: if I am not for myself, who will be for me? And if I am only for myself, what am I? And if not now, when? The first question makes room for caring for yourself. The second keeps it from shrinking into selfishness. Rightly, then, means both. Loving yourself enough to rest, to eat, to forgive your own mistakes, and remembering that everyone else is doing the very same, from the inside.
screen: `THE KING AND QUEEN MALLIKA.` · `SO, HARM NO ONE.` · `AS THYSELF.` · `HILLEL'S THREE QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `LOVING YOURSELF RIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow down by itself. Place a hand on your chest or your stomach, wherever feels natural. Feel the warmth of it. Notice whatever wish to be well is there: rested, safe, understood. A wish like that isn't selfish. It's simply human. Now, still with your hand there, let one other face come to mind, and remember that they want exactly the same thing, just as much, from the inside. Rest a while between the two. If you pray, you can ask for both of you to be well, in words your tradition already has. The bell holds the time.
Loving yourself rightly. Caring for yourself as a person worth caring for, and letting that care show you how much everyone else wants the same. Today's word.

Your line: me too. Do one kind thing for yourself today, a meal eaten sitting down, a short walk, an early night, and when you do, remember that everyone you pass wants it too. Day eight hundred seventy.

myth: in the story, the Buddha scolds the queen for being selfish
he answers with a verse: no one is dearer to anyone than themselves, so one should not harm another.
Hillel's questions include "if I am only for myself, what am I?"
his second question keeps self-care from shrinking into selfishness.
"as thyself" in Leviticus leaves the self out
the command assumes a self that is loved, and uses it as the measure.

fork.setup: you're Queen Mallika. the king asks if anyone is dearer to you than yourself. what do you say?
options: you are, my lord.
no, no one is dearer to me than myself.
I'd rather not say.
fork.reveal: she says no one is dearer than herself, and asks him the same. the Buddha doesn't scold them: he turns it into a reason not to harm anyone.

original.note: Pali: the self, oneself, the word at the center of the Buddha's verse to the king.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving yourself is selfish.
what it means: caring for yourself rightly, and seeing that everyone holds themselves just as dear.
what a scholar hears: in the Pali texts, Mallika's honest answer becomes the Buddha's reason for not harming others; Hillel's paired questions keep the same balance.

871.title: Small acts
871.hook: love is mostly in small things
871.howItsDone: Buddhists speak of gathering merit little by little through everyday good deeds, Christians read the cup of cold water as a picture of small service, and the hadith in al-Tirmidhi counts a smile or removing harm from a path among acts of charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, loving yourself rightly, and Queen Mallika's honest answer. Your line was me too. What kind thing did you do for yourself? Today, love shrinks down to fit in a cup. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

Drip. Drip. A leaky faucet over a bucket, or rain off the edge of a roof into a clay pot. Each drop is almost nothing. Nobody would bother to measure one. Leave the pot there overnight, though, and in the morning it's full to the brim. A verse in the Dhammapada, an old collection of the Buddha's sayings, uses exactly that picture, and not for water. For goodness. Three traditions speak to how small love can be and still count. Today: small acts.
screen: `DRIP. DRIP.` → `EACH DROP IS ALMOST NOTHING.` → `IN THE MORNING, A FULL POT.`

segments.voice: First, the water-pot. In Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, the verse warns against thinking lightly of good, as if it could never add up to much. Then comes the picture: "Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled." The wise, it says, become full of good the same way, gathering it little by little. No single drop fills the pot. Every drop is part of the filling. Second, a cup of water. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says that whoever gives "a cup of cold water only" to one of his little ones, in the name of a disciple, "shall in no wise lose his reward." Notice the word only. Not a banquet. Not a fortune. Just water, and cold, which in a hot land is its own kindness. The smallest gift on the table, and Jesus says it isn't lost. Third, a face. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in the collection of al-Tirmidhi, says in plain words that your smile in the face of your brother is charity. Charity, here, isn't only money. A smile counts. So does, in the same saying, guiding someone who is lost, or moving a stone out of the road. Fourth, what the three share, each in its own words. None of them says big acts don't matter. They say small ones aren't nothing. A text back. A door held. The dishes done without being asked. On an ordinary day, love often looks like that, and these teachers say it adds up.
screen: `A WATER-POT, DROP BY DROP.` · `A CUP OF COLD WATER ONLY.` · `A SMILE IS CHARITY.` · `SMALL ISN'T NOTHING.` · then, large: `SMALL ACTS.`

segments.voice: Breathe in, and breathe out slowly. As you breathe, let the day ahead come to mind, the places you'll be and the people you'll see. Now choose three small kindnesses that fit inside it. Not plans that need a calendar, just drops. A glass of water poured for someone. A real smile at the person at the counter. A message that says thinking of you. See each one clearly, one at a time, the way a drop falls. If you pray, you can offer the day in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Small acts. Kindnesses too small to measure one by one, the drop, the cup of water, the smile, that fill the pot over time. Today's word.
Your line: small things. Do three small kindnesses today, and don't wait for any of them to feel important. Count them if you like, drop by drop. Day eight hundred seventy-one.

a cup of cold water only

the saying counts a smile, guiding the lost and moving a stone from the road.
the Dhammapada compares gathering good to a pot filling with drops
"even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled."
in Matthew, the gift must be a large one to be rewarded
"a cup of cold water only" shall in no wise lose its reward.

fork.setup: a stranger looks lost in the street, and you have nothing to give but a few seconds. in the saying recorded by al-Tirmidhi, what counts as charity here?
options: nothing, without money it doesn't count.
a smile and showing them the way.
only a prayer for them later.
fork.reveal: the saying counts a smile as charity, and guiding someone who is lost too. the smallest gifts are on the list.

trapdoor: what you thought: love means big gestures.
what it means: love is mostly carried in small acts, and small acts add up.
what a scholar hears: Dhammapada 122's water-pot, Matthew 10:42's cup of cold water, and Tirmidhi's smile as charity, three texts making the same small point in their own words.

872.title: Listening as love
872.hook: listening may be love's most common form
872.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema, which opens with the word hear, in daily prayer; in Jewish mourning, by custom, visitors to a house of mourning wait for the mourner to speak first, and people on many paths practice listening as a form of care in chaplaincy and friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, small acts: a water-pot filled drop by drop. Your line was small things. Which of your three kindnesses surprised you? Today, a small act that costs nothing but attention. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

Halfway through a friend's story, a sentence starts forming. A better story. A piece of advice. The time the same thing happened to me. The friend is still talking, but the mind has already left the room to rehearse. It's a moment with two sides: the one waiting to speak, and the one who can tell they're not really being heard. Two old texts, from the letter of James and from the book of Job, point at another way to be in a conversation. Today: listening as love.
screen: `A SENTENCE STARTS FORMING.` → `THE MIND LEAVES THE ROOM.` → `ANOTHER WAY TO BE THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the order of things. The letter of James, in the King James Bible, puts it in a single line: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Swift to hear comes first. Not clever to answer. Not quick with advice. The letter puts the ears ahead of the mouth. Second, a picture of it done well. In the book of Job, everything has been taken from Job: his children, his health, his wealth. Three friends come to comfort him, and at first they do something remarkable. "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." They don't explain. They don't fix. They sit on the ground and stay. Third, what happens next. Eventually the friends start talking, and they talk for chapters, explaining why this must have happened to him. Some readers notice that the friends were at their best in the silence, and went wrong when they started to speak. At the end of the book, the text says God is not pleased with what they said about him. Fourth, a word from Hebrew that holds all of this. A prayer said in Jewish worship, from the book of Deuteronomy, begins with Shema, hear, or listen. In that prayer, listening comes first. Put it together, and listening isn't a pause before the real love begins. It can be the love. Giving someone your full attention says, without a single word, you matter enough for me to stop.
screen: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `THEY SAT WITH HIM ON THE GROUND.` · `WRONG WHEN THEY STARTED TO SPEAK.` · `SHEMA: HEAR.` · then, large: `LISTENING AS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or let them rest low. For this sit, just listen. Start with the farthest sound you can hear: traffic, wind, a distant voice. Then something closer: the room, a hum, a clock. Then the closest of all, your own breath. Don't name the sounds or judge them. Let them arrive and leave. When your mind starts composing something to say, notice it, and come back to listening. This is the same muscle a friend needs from you. If you pray, you can listen in your own tradition's way. The bell holds the time.
Listening as love. Giving someone full attention without rushing to answer, the way Job's friends sat with him on the ground. Today's word.
Your line: just listen. In one conversation today, let the other person finish completely before you start to answer, and don't plan your reply while they talk. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

trapdoor: what you thought: listening is just waiting your turn.
what it means: full attention, without rushing to fix or answer, as a form of love.
what a scholar hears: James 1:19's order of ears before mouth, and Job's friends who did best sitting in silence and went wrong when they spoke.

873.title: Love and grief
873.hook: grief is love with nowhere to go, as many say
873.howItsDone: Traditions mark grief in their own ways: Jewish mourners sit shiva, Christians hold funerals and remember the dead in prayer, Muslims pray the funeral prayer and visit the family, Hindus and Sikhs each hold their own rites and recitations for the departed, and many Buddhists chant and make offerings in their name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening as love: Job's friends sitting on the ground in silence. Your line was just listen. Who did you let finish? Today stays close to that silence, with a harder kind of love. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

A coat still hangs by the door, months later. Nobody wears it. Nobody can move it either. A phone still holds a voicemail that never gets deleted. A recipe card sits in a drawer in handwriting that won't come again. These are small things, and they can stop a person cold in the middle of an ordinary afternoon. People sometimes put it this way: grief is love with nowhere to go. In the Gospel of John, there's a scene where grief and love show up together, side by side, in the same breath. Today: love and grief.
screen: `A COAT STILL BY THE DOOR.` → `A VOICEMAIL NEVER DELETED.` → `GRIEF AND LOVE, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the scene. Jesus has a friend named Lazarus, in the village of Bethany, with his sisters Martha and Mary. Lazarus falls sick and dies before Jesus arrives. When Jesus comes, Mary falls at his feet weeping, and the people with her are weeping too. Jesus asks where they have laid him. And then comes a verse of two words, in the King James text: "Jesus wept." Second, what the onlookers see. They don't say, look how sad he is. The text has them say, "Behold how he loved him!" Standing by a grave, they read his tears as love. That's the whole idea of today in one line: the grief was the shape the love took. Third, the surprise. In John's story, Jesus is about to call Lazarus out of the tomb. The ending is close. And still he weeps. Some Christians see in it that hope doesn't cancel grief. Even with a happy ending moments away, the loss is real and it's honored with tears. Fourth, the idea from the hook. Grief is love with nowhere to go. It's a line people say, not a scripture, but it fits the scene. Love that used to have a phone number, a chair at the table, a person to reach. Now it has nowhere to land, so it comes out as tears, as a coat that can't be moved. Seen this way, grief isn't a sign that something went wrong with you. It's evidence of what was there. Different traditions hold death and what follows it in very different ways, and this lesson won't choose among them. But on any path, the tears can be read the way the people at Bethany read them.
screen: `A FRIEND NAMED LAZARUS.` · `BEHOLD HOW HE LOVED HIM.` · `HE WEEPS ANYWAY.` · `LOVE WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · then, large: `JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move at its own pace. If it feels right today, bring to mind one grief. It might be a person, or a place, a pet, a time of life, a friendship that ended. If nothing comes, that's fine too: just sit with the breath. If something does come, let it be there without fixing it. Then, quietly, say to yourself: it was love. Let that sentence sit beside the grief, not replacing it. If tears come, let them. If you pray, you can hold this one in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Love and grief. Two things that can turn out to be one, the way the onlookers at Bethany saw tears and said, behold how he loved him. Today's word.
Your line: it was love. Today, if an old loss catches you off guard, don't scold yourself for it. Name it for what it is, and let it be a kind of remembering. Day eight hundred seventy-three.

"grief is love with nowhere to go" is a line from scripture

fork.setup: you're standing with the crowd at Bethany, and you see Jesus weeping at his friend's grave. what do the people say?
options: he must have no hope.
behold how he loved him!
he came too late.
fork.reveal: the text has them say, "behold how he loved him!" his tears are read as love. some others there ask whether he couldn't have kept his friend from dying.

trapdoor: what you thought: grief means something went wrong.
what it means: grief is the shape love takes when the person isn't there to receive it.
what a scholar hears: in John 11, Jesus weeps just before he calls Lazarus from the tomb, and the onlookers read the tears as love.

874.title: St Valentine
874.hook: an early Christian martyr whose day became about love, 14 February
874.howItsDone: Some churches still keep a feast of St Valentine on February 14, and around the world the day is marked by giving cards, notes and flowers to partners, friends and family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, love and grief: Jesus wept, and the people said, behold how he loved him. Your line was it was love. Today begins a few days of love, the festivals people keep for it. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

Red paper hearts taped to a classroom window. A drugstore aisle that turns pink overnight. Roses by the bucket, and a wait for every table. In plenty of countries, February the fourteenth has become the day for saying I love you out loud. But the name on the day belongs to someone the cards never mention: a Christian remembered as a martyr, whose story is mostly lost. Today starts a short run of days of love, kept by different traditions. First: St Valentine.
screen: `RED PAPER HEARTS.` → `A NAME ON THE DAY.` → `A STORY MOSTLY LOST.`

segments.voice: First, the honest part. Tradition says Valentine was a Christian in the early centuries of the church, in or near Rome, who was put to death for his faith. Beyond that, the record is thin. Old church lists remember more than one martyr named Valentine, and it isn't clear whether the stories are about one man or several. When the sources are this quiet, it's worth saying so. Second, the stories people tell. One legend has him marrying couples in secret when marriage was forbidden to soldiers. Another has him healing his jailer's daughter and leaving her a note signed, from your Valentine. These are stories, told and retold, not facts anyone can check, and they're loved anyway. Third, how a martyr's day became a lovers' day. Long afterward, the English poet Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a poem, the Parliament of Fowls, set on Saint Valentine's day, when every bird comes to choose its mate. Some scholars think that poem, and others like it, helped tie the saint's day to romance. Nobody can say for certain how the change happened. Fourth, what's left when the legends are set aside. A person remembered by Christians as faithful unto death. And a day the world uses to say, plainly, I love you. Some churches still remember him on that day. And one custom of the modern day is a small one, and it fits the legend of the note: write it down. Tell someone, on paper, what they mean to you.
screen: `A MARTYR, THE RECORD THIN.` · `THE STORIES PEOPLE TELL.` · `CHAUCER'S BIRDS CHOOSE MATES.` · `WRITE IT DOWN.` · then, large: `ST VALENTINE.`

segments.voice: Settle into your seat. Bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear from you. A partner, a parent, a friend, a teacher, a child. Not necessarily the obvious one. Let their face come clear. Now, still sitting, let one true sentence form about what they mean to you. Plain is better than clever. Something like, you made that year easier, or I think of you when. Hold the sentence until it feels right. After the bell, you can write it down. If you pray, you can give thanks for them in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
St Valentine. A Christian remembered as a martyr, little known for certain, whose day became a day for telling people you love them. Today's word.
Your line: a note. Today, write a short note to someone, on paper or on a screen, with the sentence you found in the sit. Don't wait for February. Day eight hundred seventy-four.

875.title: Tu B'Av
875.hook: the fifteenth of Av, once a day when young women danced in white in the vineyards (Mishnah Taanit 4:8)
875.howItsDone: Some Jews today mark Tu B'Av as a day of love, with weddings, matchmaking events and celebrations, and Jews who study the Mishnah read about it in tractate Taanit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, St Valentine: a martyr whose story is mostly lost, and a day for saying it on paper. Your line was a note. Who got yours? Today, a much older day of love, and the end of the week. Day eight hundred seventy-five.

Rows of vines outside Jerusalem. Young women walk out between them, all dressed in white, and begin to dance. It sounds like the opening of a romance, but it's in the Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law and teaching, at the close of a section about fast days. In the middle of all that seriousness, a rabbi stops to remember a day of pure joy. Its name is a date on the Hebrew calendar: the fifteenth of the month of Av. Today: Tu B'Av.
screen: `ROWS OF VINES.` → `ALL DRESSED IN WHITE.` → `A RABBI REMEMBERS JOY.`

segments.voice: First, the saying. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says, in plain words, that Israel had no days of joy like the fifteenth of Av and the Day of Atonement. On those days, the daughters of Jerusalem went out in white garments, and danced in the vineyards. Second, the detail that makes the passage. The white garments were borrowed, the Mishnah says, so as not to shame anyone who had none of her own. Rich or poor, nobody could tell. On a day about love, the first act was a kindness about dignity. Third, what they said. The young women called out to the young men, in plain words: lift up your eyes and see whom you choose; don't look at beauty, look at family. The Mishnah then reads a line from the Song of Songs about a king on the day of his wedding, and the gladness of his heart. Fourth, the name. Tu is the number fifteen written in Hebrew letters, and Av is the month. So the name of the holiday is simply the date. The vineyard dances belong to the past. Some Jews mark the day today as a day for love, for weddings and for matchmaking, and it is a happy turn in a month that also holds the mourning of Tisha B'Av. This week we've traced love's edges: boundaries, loving yourself, small acts, listening, grief, and a note. Tu B'Av adds one more: when love dances, nobody gets left out of the white.
